name: Quran
info: The Quran, in Arabic the 'recitation', is the central religious text of Islam, which Muslims believe was revealed by God to Muhammad over some 23 years from 610 CE, and which is also studied as a text of Arabic literature.

facts.made: Muslims hold that it is the speech of God, revealed to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel; according to tradition it was compiled under Abu Bakr and given a standard form under Uthman
facts.form: Arabic text in 114 chapters (surahs) of verses (ayat); 6,236 verses in the Hafs reading; rhymed prose; one estimate counts 77,430 words
facts.where: Read and recited worldwide; early manuscripts include the Sanaa fragments found in Yemen in 1972, and several digitised copies are held by the Cambridge University Digital Library
facts.known: believed by Muslims to be God's own speech; recited in Arabic in prayer; 114 surahs opening with the Bismillah, except the ninth; seven readings fixed by Ibn Mujahid; tafsir commentary; calligraphy and illumination; the 1924 Cairo edition

t: Muslims believe the Quran was revealed orally to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over some 23 years, from 610 CE, and was later compiled and given a standard text; modern scholars debate how and when its final form was fixed.
It has 114 chapters arranged roughly by decreasing length rather than in the order of revelation, and it is recited in Arabic in prayer, with the whole text memorised by those called hafiz.

Its meaning has been explained by centuries of commentary (tafsir), its text has been copied in many scripts and printed since the 16th century, and it has been translated into over a hundred languages.
dyk: Moses is named 136 times in the Quran, more often than any other individual, and Jesus is named more often than Muhammad is.
ev: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad receives his first revelation in the Cave of Hira on the Laylat al-Qadr
Muhammad dies; Muslims hold that the revelation was complete by this year, and tradition says the Quran did not yet exist in book form
Caliph Uthman orders a committee headed by Zayd ibn Thabit to prepare a standard text, the Uthmanic codex, and sends copies to city centres
The date Gerd R. Puin gave to the Sanaa manuscripts, whose 12,000 pieces were found in a mosque in Yemen in 1972
The Baghdad scholar Ibn Mujahid establishes seven acceptable readings of the Quran
Robert of Ketton completes the first translation of the Quran into a Western language, Latin
The first complete Quran printed with movable type is produced in Venice, for the Ottoman market
Al-Azhar University publishes the Cairo edition, which standardises Quranic orthography and became the basis of later editions

sections.origins:
The Quran is the central religious text of Islam. Muslims believe it is a revelation directly from God (Allah), delivered orally to the final prophet, Muhammad, through the angel Gabriel in instalments over some 23 years. Islamic tradition relates that the first revelation came in 610 CE in the Cave of Hira, on the Laylat al-Qadr, during one of Muhammad's retreats to the mountains, when he was 40. It continued until 11 AH/632 CE, the year of his death.

Tradition classes the revelations as Meccan, which make up two-thirds of the Quran, or Medinan, from the period 622 to 632 that followed the Hijrah, Muhammad's migration to Medina. They were first transmitted orally. Tradition holds that they began to be written down towards the end of the Meccan period, on tablets, bones and the broad, flat ends of palm leaves. Scholars agree that Muhammad did not write the revelation himself, since the Quran calls him ummi, usually understood as unlettered.

Modern Quranic studies relates the text to Rabbinic, Jewish-Christian, Syriac Christian and Hellenic literature as well as to pre-Islamic Arabia. The Quran also uses words such as hajj (pilgrimage), salat (prayer) and zakat (charity) that appear in pre-Islamic Safaitic-Arabic inscriptions.
sections.content:
The Quran describes itself as a guide for humanity (2:185). It has 114 chapters (surahs) of varying lengths, made up of verses (ayat), a word that originally means a sign. The Hafs reading has 6,236 verses. The chapters are not in chronological order but appear roughly in order of decreasing size. Each begins with the Bismillah, 'In the name of God', except the ninth; the phrase still occurs 114 times, because it also appears in 27:30, in Solomon's letter to the Queen of Sheba. Of the 114 chapters, 29 open with combinations of letters called the muqatta'at, whose meaning is debated.

Its central theme is monotheism: God is described as living, eternal, omniscient and omnipotent, and the creator of all things. About one-third of the text is estimated to concern the afterlife and the Day of Judgment. It also treats prayer, charity, fasting in Ramadan, ethical and legal matters, and the narratives of earlier prophets. Moses is named 136 times, and Abraham appears in 35 chapters. Only a small share of the verses addresses explicit legal matters, and the text sets out no complete legal code.

Its style is described as allusive: events are referred to rather than narrated. It is often called rhymed prose, with rhyme conspicuous in many early Meccan chapters, and it does not quote biblical texts directly but summarises and varies their narratives. For convenience of reading it is also divided into 30 parts (juz') and seven parts (manzil).
sections.making:
According to tradition, after Muhammad's death in 632 many of the companions who had memorised the Quran were killed by Musaylima in the Battle of al-Yamama. The first caliph, Abu Bakr, then had the text compiled into a single volume, appointing Zayd ibn Thabit, who had written down the revelation for Muhammad, from parchments, palm-leaf stalks, thin stones and men who knew it by heart. The volume passed to Muhammad's widow Hafsa bint Umar.

Around the 650s, as Islam spread beyond Arabia, conflicts arose among soldiers over differing readings. Tradition holds that the caliph Uthman (r. 644 to 656) ordered a committee headed by Zayd to prepare a standard text, the Uthmanic codex, and sent copies to various city centres. It is also believed that other versions were collected and destroyed on his orders. The historian Michael Cook notes that early Muslim accounts of this compilation sometimes contradict themselves. Muslim scholars generally take the present text to be the Qurayshi version compiled by Abu Bakr and codified by Uthman.

Scholars of Quranic studies differ more widely. Until the early 1970s non-Muslim scholars generally accepted the traditional narrative, apart from its divine source. Patricia Crone and Michael Cook question whether the book existed in any form before the last decade of the seventh century, and John Wansbrough and Yehuda D. Nevo argued that canonisation took about 200 years. Other researchers find the text more complex than a single compilation. These positions are contested, and no critical text based on manuscript evidence has been made.
sections.reception:
Muslims regard the Quran as the word of God (Kalam Allah) and as Muhammad's most important miracle, a proof of his prophethood. Whether it was created or uncreated became a fierce theological debate, and when political authority joined the discussion some scholars who opposed the official position faced persecution in the time of the caliph al-Ma'mun and the years after. Muslims believe the present text corresponds to what was revealed to Muhammad and, by their interpretation of 15:9, is protected from corruption.

Meaning is explained through tafsir, commentary, which is divided into received tafsir, passed down from Muhammad and his companions, and tafsir by opinion. Sufi and other esoteric readers add ta'wil, interpretation of an inner (batin) meaning, while Salafis and Zahiris hold that the text should be taken only at its apparent meaning. Hadiths serve as further guidance for most Muslims. The doctrine of i'jaz, the inimitability of the Quran, holds that no human speech can match it; its first works appeared in the 9th century in Mu'tazila circles, and the best known are two books by al-Jurjani (d. 1078). Some scholars, among them Theodor Noldeke, Friedrich Schwally and John Wansbrough, pointed to linguistic defects in the text.

The Baha'i Faith and the Druze also regard the Quran as holy. In worship, Surah al-Fatiha is recited in every rakat of the prayer, and some Muslims perform ritual washing before touching a copy, though this view is not universal.
sections.survival:
Before printing was widely adopted in the 19th century the Quran was transmitted in manuscripts made by calligraphers and copyists. The earliest were written in Hijazi script. Thicker strokes, traditionally called Kufic, probably appeared in the ninth century, and from the 11th century naskh, muhaqqaq and rayhani were the main styles, with Maghribi popular in North Africa and Iberia. Early manuscripts lacked diacritical marks, which allowed several readings of the same written text. In the 10th century the Baghdad scholar Ibn Mujahid fixed seven acceptable readings, chosen from 8th-century readers. The most popular today are Hafs (d. 796) and Warsh (d. 812).

In 1972, in a mosque in Sanaa, Yemen, manuscripts of some 12,000 pieces were found. They include palimpsests, pages washed to be reused. Gerd R. Puin's team dated them to the early 8th century and noted unusual verse orderings and small variations, from which Puin concluded the text was evolving. None of the codices attributed to companions such as Abdullah ibn Masud or Ubayy ibn Ka'b survives.

Woodblock printing of Quranic extracts is on record from the 10th century, used mainly for amulets, and vanished after 1444. The first complete Quran printed with movable type, made in Venice in 1537 to 1538 for the Ottoman market, was not used because it contained many errors. Printing in Arabic was prohibited in the Ottoman Empire between 1483 and 1726. The 1924 Cairo edition, published by Al-Azhar University and following the reading of Asim, became the standard for modern printings.
sections.legacy:
The Quran is widely regarded as the finest work in Arabic literature, and it has significantly influenced the Arabic language. Wadad Kadi and Mustansir Mir state that it shaped the diction, themes, metaphors and symbols of Arabic literature and gave old words new meanings. The grammarian Sibawayh's early book on Arabic grammar, al-Kitab, relied heavily on its language, and after the Quran the Arabic alphabet developed rapidly into an art form.

It inspired the arts of calligraphy and illumination. It is never decorated with figurative images, but many copies have decorative patterns in the margins, between the lines or at the start of surahs, and its verses appear on buildings, mosque lamps, metalwork and pottery.

Recitation remains a living discipline. Tajwid sets rules for pronunciation and pauses, murattal is recited at a moderate pace and mujawwad more slowly and artfully, and crowds fill auditoriums for public competitions. A person who has memorised the whole text is a hafiz.

It has also been translated widely. Persian versions of the 10th to 12th centuries are the first fully attested complete translations, Robert of Ketton's Latin version of 1143 was the first into a Western language, and George Sale produced the first scholarly English translation in 1734. In 1936 translations in 102 languages were known. Translators, Muslim and non-Muslim, continue to differ on how to render it.

summary: The Quran is the central religious text of Islam, which Muslims believe God revealed to Muhammad over some 23 years from 610 CE. Tradition gives it a standard text under Uthman, while modern scholars debate how its final form was reached. It is recited, copied, interpreted and translated worldwide.
references: Michael Cook, The Koran; A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2000)
Richard Bell, Bell's introduction to the Qurʼān (Edinburgh University Press, 1970)
Fazlur Rahman, Major Themes of the Qur'an (University Of Chicago Press, 2009)
John Wansbrough, Quranic Studies (Oxford University Press, 1977)
Michael Sells, Approaching the Qur'ān: The Early Revelations (White Cloud Press, 1999)
Neal Robinson, Discovering the Qur'an: A Contemporary Approach to a Veiled Text (SCM Press, 1996)
notes: The article gives Abu Bakr's death as 644 in one place (Compilation and preservation), though it dates his reign 632-634 elsewhere; I used only the reign dates and left out the death year.

The article gives the last verse as revealed on 18 Dhu al-Hijjah 10 AH (about February or March 632) in one place and says revelation concluded in 11 AH/632 CE in the lead; I used 632 and avoided the day.

The article says the 'Meccan' tradition and the 8th-century non-Muslim evidence imply the Quran was not fixed until about the 8th century; I did not include that claim beyond the scholars named (Crone, Cook, Wansbrough, Nevo, Puin).

Left out as not suited to a neutral profile or too loosely sourced in the article: the claim that pre-1924 variants were thrown into the Nile, the Shia hadiths on distortion, claims about the date of the Masjid al-Haram and al-Aqsa, the slavery and sharia sections, the political Islam and terrorism passage, and the Criticism section (its claims about borrowing and the Sunni and Shia narratives).

'ummi' is glossed as 'usually understood as unlettered'; the article itself says only that scholars agree Muhammad did not write the revelation because of the Quranic description of him as ummi, and elsewhere speaks of his illiteracy in the inimitability doctrine.
The article's lead says 'the finest work in Arabic literature' without naming who regards it so; I wrote 'widely regarded', as the article does.
The Hafs reading is the one the article counts 6,236 verses for; the article also notes the number varies if the bismillahs are counted separately.
Sanaa manuscript dating: the article says Puin dated them to the early 8th century, but also calls them the oldest Quranic text known 'at the time' of discovery; I attributed the date to Puin.
